strengths: Novel functional basis decoder that elegantly enables continuous forecasts sampled at arbitrary resolutions, with clear inspiration from HiPPO initialization
Strong empirical efficiency: achieves competitive or superior performance with 2.6-9.1M parameters versus 35-500M parameter baselines
Thorough evaluation methodology including identification and correction of data leakage in existing benchmarks, with separate GIFT-ZS evaluation excluding Chronos pretraining data
Comprehensive ablation studies organized by component category, confirming contributions of time-scale adjustment, parallel predictions, and basis functions
Practical contributions including causal normalization that prevents information leakage with RevIN, and parallel training scheme enabling 2000+ forecasts per sample
Strong results on Chronos-ZS benchmark (0.755 MASE with FlowState(T)-9.1M vs 0.778 for TiRex-35M)
weaknesses: Title and framing overclaim 'sampling rate invariance' - the approach requires determining s_Δ based on dataset seasonality at inference time, requiring prior knowledge of temporal characteristics; lacks clear mechanism for truly unseen sampling rates without metadata

Temporal scaling scheme (s_Δ = 24/Seasonality and L_eff = L/s_Δ) lacks rigorous justification; appears ad-hoc without analysis of why this specific relationship or sensitivity to incorrectly estimated seasonality

Full GIFT-Eval results (Table 3) show TiRex-35M achieves better MASE (0.724 vs 0.728) than FlowState(T)-9.1M despite data leakage; on no-leakage models, improvements are marginal (0.738 vs 0.750), contradicting SOTA claims; authors acknowledge incomplete analysis

Critical reproducibility gaps: number of S5 layers, hidden state sizes (P, H), learning rates, schedules, augmentation details, synthetic data methodology, hardware specifications, and training time comparisons not provided; method for computing s_Δ for each benchmark dataset unexplained
Limited evaluation scope: only 2 benchmarks (GIFT-ZS, Chronos-ZS) tested; no evaluation on standard long-range forecasting benchmarks (ETTh, Weather, Electricity) limits generalization assessment

Insufficient analysis of key design choices: ablation shows 10% performance drop without time-scale adjustment but doesn't decompose whether this is due to s_Δ scaling or other factors; different basis functions (Legendre/Fourier/Half-Legendre) show similar performance (0.733-0.737 MASE), suggesting basis choice may be less critical than presented

Sampling rate robustness tested only on Loop Seattle dataset with subsampling; Figure 3 shows baselines recover performance at common frequencies (15T, 30T, 60T) likely seen during pretraining, indicating model benefits from rate exposure rather than achieving true generalization

Continuous-time modeling claim needs qualification: method fits polynomial bases to discrete sequences and samples them rather than learning true continuous dynamics; different sampling rates extract different polynomial information, but this is not rigorously validated as continuous modeling

Incomplete isolation of contributions: parallel prediction benefits rely on SSM's inherent parallelizability (not novel); causal normalization is practical but narrow contribution; CPM/MPI adopted from TiRex; different architecture (S5 vs xLSTM) makes attributing improvements difficult

No analysis of failure modes, which datasets or conditions the model struggles with, or dataset characteristics predicting performance; missing guidance for practitioners on determining s_Δ for new domains without pretraining or metadata

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving SOTA on GIFT-ZS (0.719 MASE vs TiRex 0.733) and Chronos-ZS (0.755 vs 0.778) benchmarks with significantly smaller models (9.1M vs 35M parameters)
Comprehensive and well-designed ablation studies (Table 4) systematically validating each component's contribution
Technically sound methodology with proper handling of data leakage through GIFT-ZS subset creation and causal normalization preventing information leakage
Clear presentation with informative architectural figures and well-motivated design choices (e.g., causal RevIN for parallel training)
Practical contributions including parallel prediction training scheme applicable to other causal architectures and notable model efficiency gains
weaknesses: Core claim of 'sampling rate invariance' is overstated: relies on existing S5 discretization property (Δ̄ = e^{A·Δ}) with rescaling parameter s_Δ; dataset-specific seasonality-based scaling (s_Δ = 24/Seasonality) contradicts automatic invariance framing and requires manual tuning

Limited evaluation of sampling rate robustness: single dataset (Loop Seattle) with degraded performance at common frequencies (15T, 30T, 60T), suggesting robustness advantage vanishes on seen distributions; no truly out-of-distribution frequency evaluation
'Foundation model' framing unsupported: evaluated only on two zero-shot forecasting benchmarks without evidence for generalization to diverse domains or downstream tasks expected of foundation models
Continuous-time representation benefit undemonstrated: while internal representation is continuous, outputs remain discrete samples; no evidence of practical advantages over discrete decoders

Individual technical contributions are incremental: S5 encoder is existing work, FBD is straightforward basis function combination (Eqs. 3-5), parallel training relates to existing curriculum learning, causal normalization is necessary bookkeeping; loose connection between claimed HiPPO inspiration and actual mechanism

Ablation shows basis function choice has minimal impact (Fourier 0.736, Half-Legendre 0.737 vs Legendre 0.733 MASE), suggesting the specific polynomial basis is not critical, yet this choice remains unjustified
Ad-hoc design choices lack ablation: seasonality-based temporal scaling and effective length computation (L_eff = L/s_Δ) are manually configured without exploring alternatives or sensitivity analysis

Experimental details insufficient for reproducibility: pretraining procedure sparse (no hardware, time, convergence criteria), augmentation techniques referenced without procedural details, computational costs not discussed despite efficiency claims

Missing analysis of why FFN decoders are fundamentally inferior, no comparison to ablated S5+MLP baseline isolating FBD's isolated contribution, and no discussion of practical benefits of internal continuity (interpolation, uncertainty propagation)

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art on GIFT-ZS and Chronos-ZS benchmarks while being 4-50× smaller than competing models, demonstrating substantial practical efficiency gains
Thoughtful functional basis decoder that elegantly connects continuous-time modeling to forecasting with principled mathematical foundation
Proper attention to data leakage issues: authors carefully identify and exclude overlapping data, creating a cleaner GIFT-ZS benchmark different from prior work
Well-designed parallel forecasting training scheme with proper causal normalization (running statistics) to prevent information leakage, enabling efficient training on diverse context lengths

Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies (Table 4) clearly showing value of each component, robustness testing on Loop Seattle across sampling frequencies, and evaluation with two pretraining corpora
Clear presentation with intuitive figures explaining the architecture and training scheme; sufficient implementation details for reproduction
Causal normalization properly prevents information leakage in parallel forecasting, a non-obvious technical contribution
weaknesses: Core claim of 'sampling rate invariance' is overstated: the model requires manually setting scale factor s_∆ based on seasonality rather than achieving automatic adaptation; authors acknowledge 'determining a suitable scale factor for each dataset'

Limited evaluation of sampling rate robustness: only Loop Seattle dataset tested; model shows degraded performance at common frequencies (15T, 30T, 60T) seen during training, contradicting invariance claims
Unclear whether sampling rate adaptation comes from SSM discretization property (which exists in prior work) or from the FBD; paper does not clearly disentangle these contributions

Moderate novelty: S5 encoder is existing work (Smith et al. 2023), FBD inspired by HiPPO (Gu et al. 2020), parallel forecasting is natural extension; primary contribution is engineering combination rather than fundamentally new techniques

Benefit of parallel forecasting not clearly quantified: 2028 forecasts per sample vs. 1 is dramatic increase, but breakdown between 'more data,' regularization, and context diversity is unclear; ablation conflates these factors

Seasonality-based scale factor is heuristic and dataset-dependent: no guidance on automatic seasonality detection, handling datasets without clear seasonality, or sensitivity of performance to s_∆ selection

Evaluation setup (modified GIFT-ZS excluding 3 Solar tasks and Chronos-overlapping tasks) differs from Auer et al. (2025), making direct comparison with published benchmarks difficult and reducing reproducibility

Ablation studies incomplete: basis function variants (Fourier, Half-Legendre) yield similar results (0.733-0.737 MASE), suggesting continuous representation choice matters less than claimed; ablations only on 2.6M model

Causal normalization via running statistics (Eqs. 8-10) may be unstable on short sequences with few samples; no discussion of variance estimation stability or ablation comparing causal vs. standard normalization

Missing practical details: no reporting of training time or computational costs compared to baselines, no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, unclear how multivariate performance scales with dimensionality

strengths: Novel functional basis decoder combining S5 encoder with continuous forecasting enables sampling-rate equivariance with formal theoretical justification (Proposition B.3, O(max{∆,∆'}) error bound)
Strong empirical results achieving SOTA on GIFT-Eval (0.701 MASE) while using 10.7× fewer parameters than TimesFM-2.5; competitive performance on standard benchmarks (7/8 best MAE)

Comprehensive experimental validation including systematic ablations (Table 2) demonstrating importance of each component, robustness testing across unseen sampling rates (Figure 4), and qualitative analysis (Figures 5-7)

Thoughtful technical solutions to practical problems: causal normalization preventing information leakage in parallel forecasting, time noise for smooth forecasts, efficient parallel training generating 4,076 forecasts per sample
Excellent reproducibility documentation with detailed hyperparameters (Table 7), data sources (Tables 4-6), architecture specifications, preprocessing details, and training infrastructure description
weaknesses: Fundamental limitation: univariate-only processing prevents capturing cross-channel dependencies and covariate information, significantly restricting practical applicability to multivariate forecasting problems; authors acknowledge but offer no solution

Manual scale factor selection via heuristic (Algorithm 1) introduces user burden; automatic selection degrades performance (0.725→0.746 MASE), and sensitivity analysis (Figure 9) shows meaningful degradation with incorrect factors

Theoretical gaps in multi-layer analysis: equivariance proof only for single-layer SSM; multi-layer error tracking (Appendix B.1, Eqs. 53-54) relies on informal arguments and unvalidated assumptions about uniform stability/Lipschitz bounds; approximation constants in error bound (Eq. 45) could be large but unmeasured

Main results use only seed 0 with unsupported claim of 'no major performance variation'; ablations use only 3 seeds; only 0.6% improvement over TimesFM-2.5 on GIFT-Eval raises questions about statistical significance

Incomplete analysis of design choices: selective ∆_E hurts performance (0.749 vs 0.725 MASE) without explanation; limited basis function exploration (only Legendre and Fourier); necessity of FBD not immediately clear if encoder produces invariant representations

strengths: Well-engineered combination of S5 encoder with functional basis decoder, demonstrating attention to details like causal normalization
Achieves state-of-the-art on GIFT-Eval benchmark with significant parameter efficiency (18.6M vs 200M+ for competitors)
Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 2) systematically quantifying contribution of each component
Provides formal theoretical analysis of approximate sampling-rate equivariance with explicit error bounds
Extensive experimental documentation with detailed hyperparameters, preprocessing, and training setup
Solid presentation and clear motivation for architectural choices
weaknesses: Core novelty is limited: S5 encoder is existing, basis function decoding is well-established, parallel forecasting is not novel. Sampling-rate equivariance framing is main novelty but relies on repackaged components
Sampling-rate equivariance—the central contribution—is only approximate with error bounded by ZOH discretization. Practical significance of the error is never empirically quantified

Validation of key claim severely limited: only ONE dataset (ETT1) tested for robustness to unseen sampling rates, with only 9 sampling intervals. No evidence this property matters across diverse domains

Multi-layer equivariance analysis incomplete: formal proof only covers single-layer case; full multi-layer analysis relies on informal error propagation reasoning (Eqs. 53-54), insufficient for central claim
Marginal empirical improvements: GIFT-Eval shows 0.57% margin over TimesFM-2.5, with smaller variant (10.6M) essentially tied. Standard benchmarks show inconsistent advantages

Scale factor selection critically relies on manual heuristics (Algorithm 1 requiring domain knowledge input); automatic version degrades performance by 3%. Undermines claimed benefit of adaptation to different sampling rates
No multi-variate support: processes channels independently in uni-variate mode, severely limiting practical applicability since most real applications are inherently multi-variate with dependencies
Practical motivation unclear: sampling-rate adaptation is presented as key benefit, but most practitioners work with fixed sampling rates. When is this property actually needed?
Weak justification for design choices: Legendre polynomial selection justified only for HiPPO consistency; time noise mechanism unclear; basis function count selection unprincipled

Limited evaluation of key claims: Figure 2 shows single anecdotal example; Figure 8 correlations are expected given ZOH discretization design; no direct empirical measurement of equivariance error across datasets

strengths: Novel sampling-rate equivariant architecture combining SSM encoder with functional basis decoder, enabling continuous-time modeling and dynamic timescale adjustment without retraining
State-of-the-art GIFT-Eval results (MASE 0.701) achieved with substantially fewer parameters (18.6M) compared to TimesFM-2.5 (200M), demonstrating strong parameter efficiency
Demonstrated robustness to unseen sampling rates (Figure 4) with consistent outperformance of baselines at non-standard frequencies, addressing a practically important problem
Rigorous theoretical analysis of sampling-rate equivariance (Section 4, Appendix B) with formal ZOH discretization bounds and clearly stated assumptions

Comprehensive experimental validation including detailed ablation studies isolating component contributions, parallel prediction training impact, and empirical equivariance verification via hidden state correlation
Clever design of causal normalization to prevent information leakage in parallel forecasting training scheme, enabling efficient training on variable context lengths
Competitive performance on standard benchmarks (Table 3: best MAE on 7/8 datasets) alongside SOTA zero-shot results, showing broad applicability
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations (scale factor heuristic dependency, univariate-only processing) without overselling capabilities
weaknesses: Scale factor selection via Algorithm 1 is domain/frequency-dependent heuristic; automatic selection degrades performance (0.725→0.746 MASE), undermining 'no retraining' claim and suggesting scale factor still requires tuning
Sampling-rate equivariance is provably approximate with error O(max{∆,∆'}) bounded by unknown constants; multi-layer error analysis lacks explicit bounds and relies on informal recursion arguments
No empirical quantification of actual approximation errors across different sampling rate pairs or systematic equivariance validation across multiple datasets; Figure 2 shows only single example

Critical design choice unexplained: selective ∆_E parameter hurts performance (0.749 MASE) contrary to S6/Mamba results, contradicting intuition and deserving investigation

Evaluation setup potential confound: effective length formula (L_eff = L/s_∆) assigns longer actual contexts to datasets with larger seasonality, conflating length benefits with sampling-rate adaptation

Incomplete equivariance validation relying on indirect evidence (hidden state correlation); no systematic study of equivariance error magnitudes or analysis of when continuous-time assumption breaks down
Missing ablations on basis function choices and limited exploration of alternatives; time noise regularization (τ=0.1) motivated only in appendix despite clear training importance
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned, main results use single random seed (0), and critical architectural details scattered across main text and appendices
